title: Enhancing science learning through choice and prior knowledge: a mixed-methods study on fluvial processes using a stream table

authors.name: Shing-Fung Chung
authors.affiliation_first: WWF Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China

abstract.text: Background: Learning in science often hinges on the interplay between individual background and the degree of autonomy provided in the learning environment. Purpose: This study applied Falk & Dierking’s Contextual Model of Learning and investigates the impact of two personal contextual factors – prior knowledge and degrees of choice control – on students’ learning outcomes and engagement during a hands-on science activity.Sample, design and methods Utilizing a ‘stream table’ as a pedagogical technological tool, a sample of 36 university students participated in simulated experiments on fluvial processes. A mixed-methods factorial design was employed, structuring participants into six subgroups based on the timing of instruction (prior vs. post-lesson) and three degrees of choice control (No, Limited and Free Choice). Data collection integrated pre- and post-questionnaires, video observations and semi-structured interviews. Results: Quantitative results indicate that while both prior-lesson and post-lesson groups showed significant improvement in interest (p < 0.01) and knowledge (p < 0.01), students with prior lessons demonstrated a significantly higher frequency in using correct scientific terminology during the activity (U = 27, p < 0.05). Qualitatively, the findings reveal that a ‘Limited Choice’ environment fosters the highest level of collaborative problem-solving and meaningful application of prior experience compared with ‘No Choice’ settings. Conversely, ‘Free Choice’ stimulated the greatest curiosity and creativity but often led to off-topic engagement. Conclusion: These findings suggest that balancing instructional guidance with limited choice offers particular pedagogical affordances for supporting collaborative engagement and conceptual integration, helping learners meaningfully connect personal experiences with hands-on technological tasks.
